entries.name: Angular
entries.use_for: Batteries-included TypeScript framework for web apps, with routing, forms, DI and SSR.
entries.why: Google-maintained, opinionated and stable; strong fit for large teams and enterprise apps.
entries.summary: TypeScript platform for building web apps, with a component and template system, forms, routing, dependency injection, SSR and Angular Elements. Maintained by Google.
entries.best_for: Large, long-lived applications and enterprise teams that value an opinionated, batteries-included structure.
entries.not_for: Steep learning curve and verbose compared with lighter libraries. Overkill for small sites or content pages.

entries.name: ASP.NET Core
entries.use_for: Build cross-platform web apps and APIs in .NET
entries.why: Microsoft's full-stack .NET framework: MVC, Razor Pages, Blazor, minimal APIs and SignalR.
entries.summary: Open-source, cross-platform .NET framework for web apps, APIs and mobile backends: MVC, Razor Pages, Blazor, minimal APIs and SignalR, with modular components.
entries.best_for: C#/.NET teams building web apps, REST APIs, realtime services or Blazor UIs on Windows, Linux or macOS.
entries.not_for: Requires the .NET stack; not for teams in other ecosystems. Breadth of options (MVC, Razor, Blazor) can be confusing for simple needs.

entries.name: Astro
entries.use_for: Build content-driven websites with islands architecture and any UI framework.
entries.why: Ships minimal JS by default; excellent for marketing sites, blogs and docs.
entries.summary: Astro is a website build tool for the modern web that aims to pair a strong developer experience with lightweight output. The MIT-licensed monorepo holds the core astro package plus its official integration packages, each with its own release notes.
entries.best_for: Building content-focused websites such as blogs, docs or marketing pages where you want lightweight output and a JavaScript build tool with official integrations.
entries.not_for: Not a backend or workflow tool. The README itself is a short directory of packages; most usage guidance lives in the external documentation site.

entries.name: Dioxus
entries.use_for: Full-stack Rust app framework for web, desktop and mobile with a React-like API.
entries.why: Very active Rust UI framework; one codebase across web, desktop and mobile with hot reload.
entries.summary: Rust framework for building web, desktop and mobile apps from one codebase with a React-like, signals-based API, hot reloading, server functions and a CLI for bundling.
entries.best_for: Rust developers wanting a single full-stack Rust UI across platforms.
entries.not_for: Requires Rust and a smaller ecosystem than JS frameworks. Mobile and desktop rendering paths are younger than mature alternatives.

entries.name: Django
entries.use_for: Full-stack Python web framework with ORM, admin panel, auth, forms and templating built in.
entries.why: The most widely used Python web framework; batteries included, very stable, huge ecosystem and excellent docs.
entries.summary: High-level Python web framework with ORM, admin site, authentication, forms and templating built in, aimed at rapid, clean development with extensive docs.
entries.best_for: Database-backed Python web apps, CMS-style sites and admin-heavy products where batteries-included matters.
entries.not_for: Monolithic and synchronous-leaning by tradition; for tiny APIs or async-first services, FastAPI or Flask may be lighter.

entries.name: Gatsby
entries.use_for: Build React-based static and hybrid sites with a data layer
entries.why: Mature React SSG with a GraphQL data layer and a large plugin ecosystem for content sites.
entries.summary: React-based framework combining static generation with dynamic rendering, pulling data from many sources through a data layer and plugins.
entries.best_for: Maintaining existing Gatsby content sites that rely on its plugin and data ecosystem.
entries.not_for: Build times grow with site size, and the ecosystem has lost momentum versus Next.js and Astro; consider alternatives for new projects.

entries.name: htmx
entries.use_for: Add AJAX, SSE and partial page updates through HTML attributes
entries.why: Leading hypermedia approach; pairs with any backend
entries.summary: Small, dependency-free library that gives HTML attributes access to AJAX, CSS transitions, WebSockets and server-sent events, enabling partial page updates driven by server-rendered HTML.
entries.best_for: Adding interactivity to server-rendered apps with any backend without a JS build or SPA framework.
entries.not_for: Not suited to complex client-side state or offline-first apps. Server must return HTML fragments.

entries.name: Hugo
entries.use_for: Very fast static site generator in a single binary
entries.why: Most-starred static site generator; builds thousands of pages in seconds
entries.summary: Static site generator in Go distributed as a single binary, with templating, content management and asset pipelines, known for very fast builds.
entries.best_for: Blogs, documentation and large content sites needing fast builds and simple hosting.
entries.not_for: Go template syntax has a learning curve, and it is not for dynamic server-rendered apps. Some features need extended or Dart Sass builds.

entries.name: Laravel
entries.use_for: Full-stack PHP web framework
entries.why: Most popular PHP framework with a large first-party ecosystem
entries.summary: Core code of the Laravel PHP framework: routing, dependency injection container, sessions and cache backends, database ORM and migrations, queues and more with expressive syntax.
entries.best_for: Full-stack PHP web apps and APIs with a large first-party ecosystem.
entries.not_for: PHP only and convention-heavy. This repo is the framework core; start new apps from the main laravel/laravel skeleton instead.

entries.name: Next.js
entries.use_for: Full-stack React framework with SSR, static generation, server components and API routes.
entries.why: The most used React framework; huge ecosystem and first-class deployment support.
entries.summary: Full-stack React framework adding server-side rendering, static generation, server components and API routes, with Rust-based tooling for builds.
entries.best_for: Production React sites and apps needing SEO, hybrid rendering and strong hosting support.
entries.not_for: React only and increasingly complex (app router, caching). Overkill for simple static pages and best experienced on Vercel-like platforms.

entries.name: Nuxt
entries.use_for: Full-stack Vue framework with SSR, file routing and server routes.
entries.why: The standard Vue meta-framework with a large module ecosystem.
entries.summary: Full-stack Vue framework with SSR, static and hybrid rendering, file-based routing, data fetching, SEO helpers, auto-imports and server routes.
entries.best_for: Vue apps and sites needing SSR, SEO and a module ecosystem.
entries.not_for: Vue only. Smaller scope than React meta-frameworks in some areas, and SSR adds server complexity for purely client apps.

entries.name: Phoenix
entries.use_for: Full-stack Elixir web framework with LiveView for realtime server-rendered UIs.
entries.why: Proven productivity and scalability; LiveView builds interactive apps without a JS SPA.
entries.summary: Elixir web framework with LiveView for realtime, server-rendered interactive UIs, plus channels and a mix-based project generator.
entries.best_for: Realtime, high-concurrency apps and teams wanting interactive UIs without a JS SPA.
entries.not_for: Requires Elixir/Erlang knowledge and a smaller hiring pool and ecosystem than mainstream stacks.

entries.name: Quasar
entries.use_for: Vue framework for building SPAs, SSR sites, PWAs and hybrid apps from one codebase.
entries.why: Ships a large Material component set plus build targets for web, mobile and desktop.
entries.summary: Vue framework that builds SPAs, SSR/SSG sites, PWAs, browser extensions, hybrid mobile apps and Electron apps from one codebase, with a large Material component set.
entries.best_for: Vue teams wanting one codebase across web, mobile (Capacitor/Cordova) and desktop.
entries.not_for: Vue only with its own CLI and component conventions; a heavier commitment than using plain Vue plus a UI kit.

entries.name: React
entries.use_for: Build component-based user interfaces for web apps
entries.why: The most used frontend library; foundation of Next.js, React Router and more
entries.summary: JavaScript library for building user interfaces with declarative, component-based views. Foundation for frameworks such as Next.js and React Router.
entries.best_for: Interactive UIs of any size where you choose your own routing, data and build tooling or use a framework on top.
entries.not_for: Only the view layer: routing, data fetching and SSR need other tools or a framework. Not ideal for static content sites.

entries.name: React Router (Remix)
entries.use_for: Routing library and full-stack React framework (Remix merged into v7)
entries.why: The most used React router; its framework mode is the successor of Remix
entries.summary: Multi-strategy React router usable minimally as a library or maximally as a framework (Remix merged into v7), with loaders, actions and SSR.
entries.best_for: React SPAs needing routing, or full-stack React apps using framework mode as the Remix successor.
entries.not_for: React only. Framework mode has its own conventions and tooling; Next.js has a bigger ecosystem and hosting integration.

entries.name: react-admin
entries.use_for: Build admin SPAs on top of REST or GraphQL APIs
entries.why: Long-standing React framework for admin UIs with data providers, auth, i18n and Material UI components.
entries.summary: Frontend framework for building admin single-page apps on REST or GraphQL APIs using React, TypeScript and Material UI, with data providers, auth, i18n and ready CRUD components.
entries.best_for: Admin panels and back-office UIs on top of existing APIs.
entries.not_for: Tied to Material UI styling and React; some advanced features are in the paid Enterprise Edition. Not for public marketing sites.

entries.name: Refine
entries.use_for: Build internal tools, admin panels and B2B CRUD apps in React
entries.why: Headless React meta-framework with data providers for REST/GraphQL/Supabase, auth and access control; UI-agnostic.
entries.summary: Headless React meta-framework for CRUD-heavy apps, with data providers for REST, GraphQL, Supabase and more, plus auth, access control and UI-agnostic hooks.
entries.best_for: Internal tools, admin panels and B2B dashboards where you want to choose your UI kit.
entries.not_for: React only; headless means you wire UI yourself. Some enterprise features and an AI agent are tied to Refine's commercial offering.

entries.name: Remix
entries.use_for: Build full-stack web apps on web-standard APIs
entries.why: The Remix team's full-stack framework (v3) built on web Fetch APIs; companion to React Router.
entries.summary: Remix 3 repository: a full-stack framework in active development built on web-standard Fetch APIs, with principles such as model-first development and optimization for LLMs. Companion to React Router.
entries.best_for: Experimenting with the new Remix direction on web standards.
entries.not_for: Under active development, so not a stable production choice. For current Remix-style apps use React Router framework mode.

entries.name: Ruby on Rails
entries.use_for: Full-stack MVC web framework for Ruby
entries.why: The defining full-stack framework; Hotwire for modern UIs
entries.summary: Full-stack Ruby MVC web framework including database-backed models, controllers and views, with generators, Hotwire for modern UIs and convention over configuration.
entries.best_for: CRUD-driven web apps and startups wanting fast development with strong conventions.
entries.not_for: Ruby only and opinionated. High-throughput or CPU-bound services may fit other stacks better; heavy JS SPAs need extra work.

entries.name: SolidStart
entries.use_for: Full-stack app framework for SolidJS.
entries.why: Official Solid meta-framework, built on Vite/Nitro with fine-grained reactivity.
entries.summary: Full-stack meta-framework for SolidJS built on Vite and Nitro. The default branch is the 2.0.0-alpha under heavy development, while 1.x is the maintained release.
entries.best_for: Solid projects wanting SSR, routing and server functions.
entries.not_for: This branch is alpha and unstable, so use the 1.x line for production. Solid-only and a smaller ecosystem.

entries.name: Svelte
entries.use_for: Compiler-based UI framework with a minimal runtime
entries.why: Much-loved compile-time framework; base of SvelteKit
entries.summary: Compiler-based UI framework that turns declarative components into efficient JavaScript that updates the DOM directly, with a minimal runtime.
entries.best_for: Small-to-medium interactive UIs and apps where bundle size and simple syntax matter; base of SvelteKit.
entries.not_for: Library-level only: routing and SSR need SvelteKit. Smaller ecosystem and hiring pool than React.

entries.name: SvelteKit
entries.use_for: Full-stack Svelte framework with routing, SSR and adapters for any host.
entries.why: Official Svelte app framework; small bundles and simple data loading.
entries.summary: Official full-stack framework for Svelte with routing, SSR, data loading and adapters for Cloudflare, Netlify, Node, static hosting and more.
entries.best_for: Svelte apps and sites needing SSR or static output with simple data loading.
entries.not_for: Svelte only; smaller ecosystem than Next.js. Adapter choice and hosting specifics must be handled per platform.

entries.name: TanStack Router / Start
entries.use_for: Fully type-safe router for React and Solid, and TanStack Start for full-stack apps.
entries.why: Best-in-class type safety for routes and search params; Start adds SSR and server functions.
entries.summary: Type-safe router for React and Solid with validated search params, loaders, caching, prefetching, nested layouts, and TanStack Start for SSR and server functions.
entries.best_for: SPAs and full-stack apps where end-to-end route and search-param type safety matters.
entries.not_for: React and Solid only. TanStack Start is newer than established frameworks, and strict typing adds setup overhead.

entries.name: Umi
entries.use_for: Enterprise React framework with routing, build and plugins
entries.why: Ant Group's pluggable React framework behind Ant Design Pro; conventional routing, SSR and micro-frontends.
entries.summary: Umi is a framework in the React community, maintained by sorrycc and a group of core maintainers. The README is brief and mostly covers maintainers, contributors and community channels, which are largely in Chinese.
entries.best_for: Teams building React applications who want an opinionated framework from the umi community, especially those comfortable with Chinese-language community support.
entries.not_for: React-only, so not for Vue, Svelte or other stacks. The README gives little feature detail, and its community channels are mainly Chinese-language, which may limit English support.

entries.name: Vike
entries.use_for: Flexible Vite-based framework for SSR/SSG apps with React, Vue or Solid.
entries.why: Modular alternative to Next/Nuxt when you want control over each part of the stack.
entries.summary: Vike positions itself as a replacement for Next.js/Nuxt, aimed at building mission-critical applications with stability and development freedom. The monorepo publishes the vike package and create-vike-core; separate repos provide vike-react, vike-vue and vike-solid bindings with add-ons such as zustand, pinia and query integrations.
entries.best_for: Building web apps when you want an alternative to Next.js or Nuxt that works with React, Vue or Solid through official vike-react, vike-vue and vike-solid packages.
entries.not_for: UI framework bindings live in separate repos, so you need to pick and add those packages. Documentation is on vike.dev rather than in the README.

entries.name: Vue
entries.use_for: Progressive framework for building web UIs
entries.why: One of the big three frontend frameworks; base of Nuxt
entries.summary: Source repo of Vue 3, a progressive framework for building web UIs. README only points to docs on vuejs.org and notes that issues are for bugs and feature requests.
entries.best_for: Interactive web UIs from small widgets to full SPAs, with Nuxt for SSR.
entries.not_for: Core only: routing, state and SSR need extra packages or Nuxt. Smaller job market than React.

entries.name: Wasp
entries.use_for: Declare a full-stack React + Node + Prisma app with auth built in
entries.why: Batteries-included framework: a config DSL generates routes, auth, jobs and typesafe RPC, cutting boilerplate.
entries.summary: Rails-like framework for React, Node.js and Prisma: a declarative config language generates routes, auth, jobs and typed RPC, with one-command deploys.
entries.best_for: Quickly building full-stack React and Node apps with auth and CRUD, such as SaaS prototypes.
entries.not_for: Locks you into its DSL and stack (React, Node, Prisma). Less flexible than assembling your own architecture.

entries.name: Yew
entries.use_for: Build frontend web apps in Rust compiled to WebAssembly
entries.why: Most popular Rust/Wasm frontend framework: component model, hooks, SSR and JS interop.
entries.summary: Rust framework for front-end web apps compiled to WebAssembly, with a macro for HTML templates, components, hooks, SSR and JS interop.
entries.best_for: Rust teams building browser UIs with Wasm.
entries.not_for: Requires Rust and Wasm toolchain with larger bundles and a smaller ecosystem than JS frameworks. Not for SEO-first content sites.
